narrative:
The model estimated a 58% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this was above the threshold used for the decision, your law school application was rejected; it means the model judged failure more likely than passing, not that failure is certain.

The strongest factor driving the denial was your third-year academic standing. Your third-year decile is 1, which stands well apart from the average of about 5.79 among accepted students, and this factor pushed most strongly toward bar exam failure. The second most important factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 2.90, it is below the accepted-student average of 3.23, but in this prediction it was the main factor working in your favor, lowering the estimated risk. The third factor was your part-time status: because you plan to study part-time while roughly 93% of accepted students were full-time, this raised the predicted risk.

To improve a future application, focus first on strengthening your upper-level academic record and ask an advisor whether delaying your application would help. Consider full-time study if feasible, build a structured bar-readiness plan, and seek preparation for retaking the LSAT. You should also request admissions feedback and reapply after showing concrete academic improvement.
